frames.narration: A job appends to /logs/clicks, and the last chunk of that file is full. The client asks the master for a new chunk. The master picks three servers: one in rack 2 and two in rack 5, and records the change in the operation log before it answers.
The master answers with the three locations and names cs12 as the primary by granting it a lease of 60 seconds. The client keeps this answer in a cache, so it will not ask again for a while.

messages.label: chunk 7: primary cs12, others cs31, cs33

frames.narration: The client pushes 4 MB of records to the nearest replica. Each server forwards the bytes down a chain as they arrive, so no server sends them more than once. Nothing is applied yet; the servers only hold the data in a buffer.
Now the client tells the primary to write. The primary gives the write the next serial number, 1041, and applies it to its own copy of chunk 7.
The primary tells both secondaries to apply the write as number 1041, so all three copies see the same order even if other clients are writing at the same moment. Both answer that they are done.
The primary reports success, and the client has appended at offset 0 of chunk 7. The data never passed through the master, which only handled two small requests.

Later cs31 loses power. Its heartbeats stop, while the other servers keep reporting. After the heartbeat timeout the master declares it dead, finds that chunk 7 and thousands of others are down to two copies, and queues them, fewest copies first.

The master picks cs58 in rack 3, a third rack, and tells it to fetch chunk 7 from cs12. Every other server is doing the same for other chunks, so cs31's whole disk is restored in minutes. The chunk is back to three copies in three racks.

Weeks later the scrubber reads chunk 7 on cs33 and block 9 fails its checksum: a bit had flipped on the disk. cs33 reports it, and the master has the chunk copied afresh from a good replica. The bad replica is deleted before any other copy is lost.
